subChunks.title: The Guild Header
subChunks.hookHtml:
The commission has arrived. Grand Archmage Solomon himself has chosen you — a proven expert in the utility arts — to build the Arcane Guild's public website from the ground up. Real work. Real decisions. Real consequences.

Every great site starts where the eye lands first: the header. It must be sticky, responsive, and immediately trustworthy. A frosted-glass effect signals craft. A single CTA signals clarity. Let's build it right.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Grand Archmage's chamber door stands open for the first time in years. He stands at the window, hands behind his back, looking over the academy grounds.

Grand Archmage Solomon: "I have reviewed two dozen candidates for this commission. You are here because your fundamentals are sound. But fundamentals are table stakes. This site will be seen by every prospective member, every partner guild, every student who might one day study under us. It must be worthy."

Sticky positioning vs fixed positioning

The header uses sticky top-0 — not fixed. This distinction matters:

  • fixed removes the element from document flow entirely. You must add padding-top to the page body equal to the header height, or content scrolls behind it. If the header height ever changes, you must update the offset.
  • sticky top-0 keeps the element in flow until it reaches the specified threshold, then sticks. No offset compensation needed. The element only sticks within its parent container.
<!-- fixed: you must compensate for it -->
<header class="fixed top-0 left-0 right-0 z-50 h-16">...</header>
<main class="pt-16">...</main>  <!-- magic number that breaks if header height changes -->

<!-- sticky: self-contained, no compensation -->
<header class="sticky top-0 z-50">...</header>
<main>...</main>  <!-- just works -->

Frosted glass effect

The combination of bg-white/95 and backdrop-blur-sm creates the frosted-glass effect used in virtually every modern header:

  • bg-white/95 — white at 95% opacity, letting a hint of the page show through
  • backdrop-blur-sm — blurs whatever is behind the element, creating the frosted effect
<!-- Full opacity — solid, boring -->
<header class="bg-white">...

<!-- Frosted glass — polished, modern -->
<header class="bg-white/95 backdrop-blur-sm">...

The hidden md:flex responsive nav pattern

This is the fundamental mobile navigation pattern. On small screens, the nav is completely hidden. At the md breakpoint (768px) it becomes a flex row.

<!-- Mobile: nav is display: none -->
<!-- Desktop (md+): nav is display: flex -->
<nav class="hidden md:flex items-center gap-8">
  <a href="#">Services</a>
  <a href="#">Work</a>
</nav>

In a real site you'd pair this with a hamburger menu button that uses md:hidden — hidden on desktop, shown on mobile — but for this exercise we focus on the desktop header structure.

Hover transitions on nav links

The transition-colors duration-200 pair is the standard formula for smooth colour transitions. Always specify duration-* — Tailwind's default of 150ms is fine for most cases, but 200ms feels slightly more premium:

<a class="text-gray-600 hover:text-indigo-600 transition-colors duration-200">
  Services
</a>

The header CTA button

The call-to-action in the header is deliberately small (px-4 py-2 rather than px-8 py-4) — it lives in a compact space and must not overpower the navigation. The rounded-lg (not rounded-full) gives it a professional, restrained shape.

Lyra the Scribe: "One detail I see juniors miss: the header CTA should be visually distinct but not shout. It is an invitation, not an advertisement. px-4 py-2, not px-8 py-4. Reserve the large CTA for the hero section where it belongs."

storyBeats.text: The letter bears the Grand Archmage's seal — the hexagonal sigil of the Arcane Guild, pressed in violet wax. Inside, a single line in Solomon's precise hand: 'The commission is yours. Build us a website worthy of the guild's legacy. Lyra will guide you.'

storyBeats.speaker: Grand Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: Every member of the Arcane Guild will point a prospective partner to this URL. Every student considering our academy will form their first impression from it. I need precision, professionalism, and craft. Not experimentation. Not cleverness. Craft.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: We start where every site starts: the header. Get this right and the rest of the page inherits its authority. A sticky header that stays present as the user scrolls communicates stability. The frosted-glass effect says: this is a modern, considered product.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: Use sticky top-0 z-50 — not fixed. Sticky keeps the header in document flow, so you don't need to compensate the page with padding-top. And bg-white/95 backdrop-blur-sm gives us that frosted glass. Clean. Simple. Right.

storyBeats.speaker: Frosted glass header
storyBeats.text: sticky top-0 z-50 bg-white/95 backdrop-blur-sm border-b border-gray-200

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: A colleague asks why you used sticky top-0 z-50 on the header rather than fixed top-0 left-0 right-0 z-50. Explain the difference between sticky and fixed positioning, and describe one practical scenario where each would be the better choice.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a sticky page header with scroll shadow from scratch. The header contains a logo on the left and two nav links on the right. It should be sticky top-0 with a z-50 to stay above content. Add a bottom shadow to signal elevation. No scaffold provided.

questions.questionHtml: What is the visual effect of combining bg-white/95 and backdrop-blur-sm on a header?
options: A frosted-glass effect where the header is slightly transparent and blurs content behind it
A solid white header with a blurred drop shadow
The header becomes invisible until hovered
The background image of the page is blurred underneath the header
questions.correctAnswer: A frosted-glass effect where the header is slightly transparent and blurs content behind it
questions.explanationHtml: bg-white/95 sets white at 95% opacity, allowing a hint of the page to show through. backdrop-blur-sm blurs everything behind the header element. Together they create the modern frosted-glass look used in macOS, iOS, and nearly every contemporary SaaS product.

questions.questionHtml: What does the class combination hidden md:flex achieve on a nav element?
options: The nav is hidden on screens narrower than the md breakpoint (768px) and displayed as flexbox on wider screens
The nav is hidden by default and shown only when a flex container is present
The nav is hidden until the user clicks a hamburger menu button
The nav becomes a grid on md screens and a flex row on larger screens
questions.correctAnswer: The nav is hidden on screens narrower than the md breakpoint (768px) and displayed as flexbox on wider screens
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind is mobile-first. hidden applies at all screen sizes. md:flex overrides it at the md breakpoint (768px) and above, switching the element to display: flex. This is the canonical pattern for a desktop navigation that collapses on mobile.

questions.questionHtml: You have a sticky header and notice that page content scrolls behind it on mobile but not desktop. The header has no explicit height set. What is the most likely cause?
options: The sticky positioning is inside a flex parent that stretches the header, preventing it from sticking
The header height changes between breakpoints and content is not accounting for it
backdrop-blur-sm only works on Chromium browsers, causing layout shifts on other browsers
z-50 is not high enough to stay above the content on mobile
questions.correctAnswer: The header height changes between breakpoints and content is not accounting for it
questions.explanationHtml: Unlike fixed, sticky headers stay in the document flow, so content below them does not overlap — this is actually sticky's advantage. If content is scrolling behind the header, the header is probably fixed not sticky, or a parent container has overflow: hidden which prevents sticky from working.

questions.questionHtml: A design spec requires a navigation link to transition smoothly to indigo when hovered, taking 200ms. Which class combination achieves this correctly?
options: hover:text-indigo-600 transition-colors duration-200
hover:text-indigo-600 animate-pulse
hover:text-indigo-600 transition duration-200
hover:text-indigo-600 transition-all duration-200 ease-in
questions.explanationHtml: transition-colors is more precise than transition-all — it only transitions colour properties, preventing any unexpected transitions on layout changes. duration-200 sets the 200ms timing. transition-all would also work here but is broader than needed. animate-pulse creates a continuous animation, not a hover transition.

subChunks.title: The Hero Section
subChunks.hookHtml:
The header is done. Solomon nodded once — that is high praise. Now comes the most important section of the entire site: the hero. Three seconds. That's how long a visitor decides whether to stay or leave. Your hero must communicate scale, craft, and a clear next step — instantly.

In this section you'll build gradient backgrounds, gradient text, multi-column layouts, and shadow effects with opacity modifiers. This is where the site comes alive.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Sable the Illuminator is already in the workspace when you arrive. Three colour swatches are pinned to the wall: deep indigo, rich purple, cool slate. She turns around with the focused energy of someone who has been thinking about this problem for hours.

Sable the Illuminator: "First impressions are not about content. They are about feeling. The visitor reads your hero and they feel either: 'This is serious work,' or they don't. We are going for deep, dark, and authoritative. Indigo-950 through purple-950 to slate-900. The gradient should feel like looking into a midnight sky over an ancient city."

Multi-stop gradient backgrounds

Tailwind's gradient system uses three classes together: direction, starting colour, and ending colour. For a three-stop gradient, add a via-* colour in the middle:

<!-- Two-stop gradient -->
<section class="bg-gradient-to-r from-indigo-600 to-purple-600">

<!-- Three-stop gradient: from → via → to -->
<section class="bg-gradient-to-br from-indigo-950 via-purple-950 to-slate-900">

The direction to-br means bottom-right (diagonal), which creates a more dynamic feel than a flat horizontal gradient.

Gradient text — the three-class recipe

This is one of the most-asked-about Tailwind techniques. Three classes must work together:

  1. bg-gradient-to-r from-indigo-400 to-purple-400 — sets the gradient as the element's background
  2. bg-clip-text — clips the background so it only shows through the text shape (not the full box)
  3. text-transparent — makes the actual text colour transparent, revealing the clipped background gradient
<span class="text-transparent bg-clip-text bg-gradient-to-r from-indigo-400 to-purple-400">
  experiences
</span>

<!-- Remove text-transparent and you get: solid black text with an invisible gradient background -->
<!-- Remove bg-clip-text and you get: a gradient rectangle behind normally-coloured text -->

All three are required. Missing any one breaks the effect in a different way.

Shadow with opacity modifier

Tailwind v3 supports arbitrary colour opacity on any utility with the / modifier syntax. This applies to shadows too:

<!-- Shadow using the brand colour at 25% opacity -->
<button class="shadow-lg shadow-indigo-500/25">
  Start a Project
</button>

<!-- This creates a glowing halo effect in the brand colour -->
<!-- Without /25 you'd get the default grey shadow -->

This technique — coloured shadows at low opacity — is how modern UIs create that "elevated" feel without harsh edges. Common values are /10, /20, /25.

Two-column responsive layout with grid

The hero uses a grid that is single-column on mobile and two-column on large screens:

<div class="grid grid-cols-1 lg:grid-cols-2 gap-16 items-center">
  <div><!-- text content --></div>
  <div class="hidden lg:block"><!-- visual element, hidden on mobile --></div>
</div>

The right column is hidden on mobile (hidden lg:block) because screen space is too tight to show a decorative visual alongside the text. This is a deliberate responsive decision, not an oversight.

The glassmorphism card

The hero card uses bg-slate-800/60 (60% opacity) and backdrop-blur-sm — the glassmorphism pattern. The border border-slate-700/50 adds a subtle edge at 50% opacity. All three create a sense of depth and layering on a dark background.

Lyra the Scribe: "Notice the eyebrow text: tracking-widest uppercase. Wide letter-spacing on all-caps small text is a classic typographic technique for creating visual hierarchy without size. It reads as a label, a category, a subtitle — before the main heading even registers."

storyBeats.text: Sable the Illuminator stands at the window, three colour swatches in hand: deep indigo, midnight purple, cool slate. She turns as you enter.

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: The hero section gets three seconds. Three seconds for a stranger to decide if they care. Colour does the heavy lifting before a single word is read. Deep, dark, authoritative — indigo-950 through purple-950. A gradient like a midnight sky over an ancient city.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: The heading needs a gradient word — one that glows in the indigo-to-purple spectrum. Three classes, in the right order: text-transparent, bg-clip-text, bg-gradient-to-r. Remove any one of them and the effect breaks. This is a recipe, not a preference.

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: And the primary CTA — give it a shadow in the brand colour, not grey. shadow-lg shadow-indigo-500/25. A 25% opacity indigo halo. It makes the button look like it's lit from within. Like it matters.

storyBeats.speaker: Gradient text — the three-class recipe
storyBeats.text: text-transparent bg-clip-text bg-gradient-to-r from-indigo-400 to-purple-400

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain how the three classes text-transparent bg-clip-text bg-gradient-to-r from-indigo-400 to-purple-400 work together to create gradient text. What would the element look like if you removed only text-transparent? What if you removed only bg-clip-text?

questions.questionHtml: Which three Tailwind classes are required to create gradient-coloured text?
options: text-transparent, bg-clip-text, bg-gradient-to-r (plus from-* / to-* colours)
text-gradient, from-indigo-400, to-purple-400
bg-gradient, text-clip, text-transparent
gradient-text, bg-clip-text, from-indigo-400
questions.correctAnswer: text-transparent, bg-clip-text, bg-gradient-to-r (plus from-* / to-* colours)
questions.explanationHtml: The gradient is set as a background with bg-gradient-to-r from-* to-*. Then bg-clip-text clips it to the text shape only. Finally text-transparent makes the actual text colour transparent, revealing the clipped gradient background behind it. All three must be present.

questions.questionHtml: You want a button shadow that glows in the brand colour (indigo-500) at low opacity, creating a subtle halo. Which class combination achieves this?
options: shadow-lg shadow-indigo-500/25
shadow-lg shadow-indigo-500 opacity-25
shadow-indigo-lg/25
glow-indigo-500 shadow-lg
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind's colour-shadow pattern requires two classes: shadow-lg sets the shadow size, and shadow-indigo-500/25 sets the colour with the opacity modifier. The /25 suffix applies 25% opacity to the shadow colour specifically — it does not affect the element itself.

questions.questionHtml: A dark hero section has body text using text-slate-300. A colleague suggests it looks "grey" and proposes using pure white (text-white) for better readability. What is the correct response?
options: text-slate-300 is the correct choice — pure white on a dark background causes eye strain and flattens the visual hierarchy. Slightly muted white preserves contrast while being easier to read at length.
text-white is always better for contrast on dark backgrounds — maximum contrast is always the goal
Use text-gray-300 instead of text-slate-300 for better cross-browser consistency
Neither — body text on dark backgrounds should use text-slate-100 at minimum per WCAG AA
questions.correctAnswer: text-slate-300 is the correct choice — pure white on a dark background causes eye strain and flattens the visual hierarchy. Slightly muted white preserves contrast while being easier to read at length.
questions.explanationHtml: Pure white on a very dark background (like slate-900) can cause eye strain with prolonged reading and removes tonal hierarchy — if everything is pure white, how do you distinguish headings from body from captions? text-slate-300 passes WCAG AA contrast on dark backgrounds and creates a natural reading hierarchy where headings (text-white) have more visual weight than body text.

subChunks.title: Services Grid
subChunks.hookHtml: The header holds attention. The hero earns trust. Now the site must communicate value. The services section answers the visitor's primary question: "What do they actually do?" Three cards. Clear hierarchy. And a hover interaction that rewards attention — a technique that requires Tailwind's most powerful compositional pattern: group and group-hover:.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Sable the Illuminator is at the whiteboard. Three rectangles sketched out — cards, clearly — each with an icon, a heading, a description, a link. She taps the icon area with the chalk.

Sable the Illuminator: "The hover on this card has to feel alive. When the card lifts, the icon changes colour. Not because the icon is hovered — because the card is. This is the group pattern. The parent watches. The child reacts. It is the difference between a UI that feels built and one that feels designed."

The group / group-hover: pattern

This is Tailwind's most elegant compositional technique. It allows a parent element's hover state to control the styles of its children:

<!-- Without group: only hover on the icon itself triggers the icon colour change -->
<div>
  <div class="bg-gray-100 hover:bg-indigo-600">⚡</div>  <!-- hover must be on the icon -->
  <h3>Frontend Engineering</h3>
</div>

<!-- With group: hovering anywhere on the card changes the icon colour -->
<div class="group hover:shadow-xl">
  <div class="bg-gray-100 group-hover:bg-indigo-600 transition-colors">⚡</div>  <!-- reacts to group hover -->
  <h3>Frontend Engineering</h3>
</div>

The reason you can't simply use hover: on the child element is that the hover target is the card (the parent), not the icon. When the user's cursor is over the heading text, the icon should still change colour. The child has no way to detect that the parent is hovered — only group/group-hover: bridges that relationship.

Ring vs border — when to use which

Both ring-* and border-* create visual outlines, but they work differently:

  • border is part of the box model. It takes up space and affects layout. Adding a border changes the element's size unless you use box-border.
  • ring is implemented with box-shadow. It renders outside (or inside) the element without affecting layout. It can be offset with ring-offset-*.
<!-- Featured card with a 2px ring at brand colour, offset from the element -->
<div class="ring-2 ring-indigo-500 ring-offset-2">
  <!-- The 2px ring sits outside the element with 2px white space between -->
</div>

<!-- Border: good for regular card borders -->
<div class="border border-slate-200">

<!-- Ring: good for focus indicators, selected states, featured highlighting -->
<div class="ring-2 ring-indigo-500">

Use border for structural card edges. Use ring for focus states, selected/featured indicators, and hover outlines that shouldn't affect layout.

transition-all for multi-property transitions

The service card uses transition-all duration-300 because multiple properties change on hover: border colour, shadow, and shadow colour. Rather than listing each individually, transition-all covers everything. Use it when 3+ properties transition simultaneously — but prefer specific utilities (transition-colors, transition-shadow) when only one or two properties change.

Hover shadow with colour and opacity

<!-- The card lifts and glows on hover —>
<div class="hover:shadow-xl hover:shadow-indigo-500/10">
  <!-- /10 means 10% opacity — very subtle glow, noticeable but not garish -->
</div>

Grand Archmage Solomon: "The featured card uses a ring, not a border. Do you understand why? A border shifts the layout when added. A ring does not. The card does not jump when we highlight it. Details like this are what separate competent work from excellent work."

storyBeats.text: Sable the Illuminator is at the whiteboard. Three rectangles sketched out — cards, clearly — each with an icon, a heading, a description, a link. She taps the icon area.

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: The services section must communicate value at a glance. Three cards. Clear hierarchy. And a hover that rewards attention. When the user hovers the card, the icon changes colour. Not because the icon is hovered — because the card is. This is the group pattern.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: The featured card uses a ring, not a border. A ring is implemented with box-shadow — it doesn't affect layout. Adding a border at render time would shift the card by 2px. A ring appears without displacing anything. On a featured card that appears highlighted among peers, that distinction is visible.

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: Add group to the card. Add group-hover:bg-indigo-600 to the icon. Now the icon reacts to the card hover. The user doesn't have to aim at the icon. The entire card surface is the target.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the Tailwind group / group-hover: pattern to a colleague who only knows basic hover states. Why can't you use a simple hover: variant on the child element (the icon) to achieve the same effect? Give a concrete example of where parent-driven hover control is necessary.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a project card with image zoom and title reveal from scratch using group and group-hover:. The card shows an image placeholder (coloured div) that scales on hover, and a title that transitions from muted to full white. No class scaffold given — apply the group pattern without guidance.

options: Adding group to a parent element allows its children to use group-hover: variants that activate when the parent (not the child) is hovered
group makes all children inherit the parent's hover state automatically without any additional classes
group-hover: is a shorthand for both the parent and child having the same hover:text-* class
group creates a CSS variable that child elements can read with var(--group-state)
questions.correctAnswer: Adding group to a parent element allows its children to use group-hover: variants that activate when the parent (not the child) is hovered
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind generates CSS like .group:hover .group-hover\:bg-indigo-600 — a descendant selector. When the element with group is hovered, all its descendants with group-hover:* classes update. This enables rich, coordinated hover effects across an entire card component.

questions.questionHtml: You have a card component that shows four properties changing on hover: border colour, shadow size, shadow colour, and background colour. Which transition utility is most appropriate?
options: transition-all duration-300
transition-colors transition-shadow duration-300
transition duration-300
transition-none — use CSS @keyframes instead for multiple properties
questions.explanationHtml: When 3+ properties need to transition simultaneously, transition-all is the pragmatic choice — it covers every transitional property. transition (without -all) only covers the CSS transition-property: color, background-color, border-color, text-decoration-color, fill, stroke, opacity, box-shadow, transform, filter, backdrop-filter — which actually covers this case too, but transition-all is more explicit and readable when you want everything.

questions.questionHtml: You need to highlight a selected card among a grid of cards, adding a 2px indigo outline without shifting the other cards or causing layout reflow. Which approach is correct?
options: ring-2 ring-indigo-500 ring-offset-2 — ring uses box-shadow which does not affect layout
border-2 border-indigo-500 — add a 2px border to the selected card
outline-2 outline-indigo-500 — outline is always outside the box
shadow-indigo-500 shadow-md — use a coloured shadow as a border substitute
questions.correctAnswer: ring-2 ring-indigo-500 ring-offset-2 — ring uses box-shadow which does not affect layout
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind's ring-* utilities use box-shadow rather than border. Box-shadow does not affect the box model — it renders outside the element without pushing other elements around. Adding a ring to a selected card does not change its size or shift neighbouring cards. A border would change the element's rendered dimensions unless box-sizing: border-box is set, but even then it visually compresses the padding.

subChunks.title: Team Section
subChunks.hookHtml:
The guild's reputation rests on its people. The team section is not a formality — Grand Archmage Solomon has made clear that it is a declaration of expertise. Four masters, four disciplines, displayed with the precision and dignity their craft deserves.

In this section you'll master object-cover for consistent avatar images, the relative/absolute positioning pattern for the online status dot, and the multi-breakpoint responsive grid.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Grand Archmage Solomon enters the workspace without announcement. He looks at the header and hero on the preview screen for a long moment. Then, without turning:

Grand Archmage Solomon: "Every commissioned work must credit its makers. In our tradition, the team section is not a courtesy — it is a declaration of who has put their name to this work. The Guild Council section must be built with the same precision as the hero. Four faces. Four titles. No ambiguity."

object-cover for consistent avatar images

Avatar images come from many sources — users upload photos of varying aspect ratios. Without proper handling, some avatars appear stretched or squished.

<!-- Without object-cover: image may appear stretched if not square -->
<img src="avatar.jpg" class="w-24 h-24 rounded-full">

<!-- With object-cover: image fills the circle, cropping from the centre -->
<img src="avatar.jpg" class="w-24 h-24 rounded-full object-cover">

object-cover maps to CSS object-fit: cover. It maintains the image's aspect ratio while filling the entire container, cropping any excess from the centre. This is why every avatar in every modern app looks correctly proportioned regardless of the original photo dimensions.

The relative/absolute positioning pattern for status dots

The online status dot sits on the bottom-right corner of the avatar. This classic UI pattern requires:

  1. A wrapper element with relative positioning to act as the positioning context
  2. The status dot with absolute positioning to place it precisely within that context
<div class="relative w-24 h-24">
  <img src="avatar.jpg" class="w-24 h-24 rounded-full object-cover ring-4 ring-white shadow-lg">
  <span class="absolute bottom-1 right-1 w-4 h-4 bg-green-400 rounded-full ring-2 ring-white"></span>
</div>

<!-- If relative is removed from the wrapper: -->
<!-- absolute is placed relative to the nearest positioned ancestor, -->
<!-- which might be the section or the body — the dot flies off the avatar -->

The ring-2 ring-white on the status dot creates a 2px white gap between the dot and the avatar image, making the green dot clearly readable even when the avatar photo has a dark edge.

ring-* on avatars vs border

Avatar frames use ring-4 ring-white rather than border-4 border-white. The reasons:

  • Ring renders outside the element via box-shadow, so the w-24 h-24 dimensions remain exact — the image size is predictable
  • Ring offset creates a clean gap between the image and a coloured outer ring, useful for hover states
  • The group-hover state changes ring-white to group-hover:ring-indigo-300 — a colour transition on a ring, not a border

Multi-breakpoint responsive grid

The team grid uses three breakpoints to progress from single column to four:

<!-- Mobile: 1 column (default) -->
<!-- sm (640px+): 2 columns — room for two avatars side by side -->
<!-- lg (1024px+): 4 columns — full row on desktop -->
<div class="grid grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4 gap-8">

The decision to skip md:grid-cols-4 (going directly to 4 at lg) is intentional — at 768px four avatars feel cramped. At 1024px there's comfortable breathing room for four cards.

Lyra the Scribe: "The text-center group on each team card is worth noting. The card has no visual background — it is transparent. The group is there purely for the group-hover ring change on the avatar. A component can be a group for behavioural reasons, not visual ones."

storyBeats.text: Grand Archmage Solomon enters without announcement. He studies the header and hero on the preview screen for a long moment — long enough that the silence becomes intentional. Then he turns.

storyBeats.text: In our tradition, work that bears the guild's name also bears the names of those who made it. The Guild Council section is not a formality. It is a declaration. Four masters, displayed with the dignity their craft has earned. Make it worthy of them.

storyBeats.text: The avatar images come from uploads — aspect ratios vary. Use object-cover so every photo fills the circle correctly, cropped from the centre. Without it, a wide landscape photo of Sable will look like she was squeezed into a test tube.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: The status dot uses relative on the wrapper and absolute bottom-1 right-1 on the dot. The wrapper must have relative — otherwise the dot looks for the nearest positioned ancestor, which might be the section container, and the dot ends up in completely the wrong position.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain how relative on the avatar wrapper and absolute bottom-1 right-1 on the status dot work together to place the dot correctly in the corner of the avatar. What would happen visually if you removed relative from the wrapper?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build an avatar with a positioned status dot from scratch using Tailwind positioning utilities. The avatar is a circular image placeholder (w-14 h-14) with a small w-3.5 h-3.5 green dot anchored to its bottom-right corner. The dot must stay in the corner regardless of the avatar size. Apply relative and absolute without any class scaffold — recall the containment relationship yourself.

questions.questionHtml: What does the object-cover class do to an <img> element that has both width and height constraints?
options: The image fills the container entirely, maintaining aspect ratio by cropping any excess from the centre
The image is scaled down to fit entirely within the container, potentially leaving whitespace
The image is stretched to fill the container, ignoring aspect ratio
The image is tiled to fill the container
questions.correctAnswer: The image fills the container entirely, maintaining aspect ratio by cropping any excess from the centre
questions.explanationHtml: object-cover maps to CSS object-fit: cover. The image is scaled proportionally until it fills the container's dimensions completely. Any parts of the image that extend beyond the container are cropped. This is why avatar images look correctly proportioned in a fixed w-24 h-24 circle, regardless of whether the original photo is landscape, portrait, or square.

questions.questionHtml: You have a notification badge that must appear at the top-right corner of an icon button. Which structure correctly positions the badge?
options: 3
3
3
questions.explanationHtml: The wrapper must have relative to create a positioning context. The badge uses absolute top-0 right-0 to anchor itself to the top-right corner of that context. Without relative on the wrapper, the badge would be positioned relative to the nearest ancestor that has position: relative/absolute/fixed/sticky — which could be anywhere in the page.

questions.questionHtml: For an avatar image frame (a circular ring that visually frames the avatar photo), which is the better choice and why: ring-4 ring-white or border-4 border-white?
options: ring-4 ring-white — ring uses box-shadow so the image dimensions stay exactly w-24 h-24, and ring-offset creates a clean gap that border cannot
border-4 border-white — borders are more widely supported and render more predictably across browsers
Both are identical in all practical respects — choose whichever you prefer
border-4 border-white — because ring uses box-shadow which doesn't work on circular elements
questions.correctAnswer: ring-4 ring-white — ring uses box-shadow so the image dimensions stay exactly w-24 h-24, and ring-offset creates a clean gap that border cannot
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind ring-* uses box-shadow to render outside the element's box model. A ring-4 avatar image stays exactly w-24 h-24 (96px) — the ring is cosmetic. A border-4 would add 8px to the rendered dimensions (4px each side), potentially misaligning the avatar with other layout elements unless box-sizing: border-box is enforced. Additionally, ring-offset-* creates a gap between the image and an outer ring — something border cannot do without extra markup.

subChunks.title: The Grand Commission
subChunks.hookHtml:
Four sections. One page. Everything you have learned — sticky headers, gradient backgrounds, gradient text, coloured shadows, the group pattern, ring highlights, multi-breakpoint grids, object-cover, absolute positioning — converges here.

The guild is watching. Grand Archmage Solomon himself will review the final page. This is the moment that separates a practitioner from an expert.

The Grand Commission is open. Demonstrate your mastery.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The guild's great hall has never been this quiet. Every lantern is lit. The full Guild Council stands in a line before the large presentation screen. Grand Archmage Solomon stands apart, hands clasped behind his back. He does not speak immediately.

Grand Archmage Solomon: "You have learned every technique this commission requires. The gradient background. The gradient text. The sticky header. The group pattern. The ring. The status dot. The responsive grids. Individually they are tools. Together, assembled with judgment and precision, they are a product. You will now assemble them."

Lyra steps forward, unrolling a parchment.

Lyra the Scribe: "I have prepared the HTML skeleton. Every section is present. Every semantic class name is applied. But the Tailwind utilities are stripped. You must restore them from memory and understanding, not from copying. The starter code has comments at each section reminding you what is required. Trust your knowledge."

What this challenge tests

This is not a recall exercise — it is a synthesis exercise. You will encounter moments where you must choose between similar approaches:

  • Sticky vs fixed for the header — you know the answer
  • Ring vs border for the featured card — you know which affects layout and which does not
  • hidden lg:block vs lg:hidden block for the hero visual — the order of mobile-first matters
  • text-transparent bg-clip-text vs just a coloured heading — you know which creates the gradient text effect

Reading the comments

Each section in the starter code has an HTML comment listing the key classes to apply. These are the same classes you applied in TWD1–TWD4. The comments are hints, not cheats — they tell you what the design requires, and you must know how to express that requirement in Tailwind.

Working methodically

Work section by section. Start with the header — it is the simplest. Then the hero. Then services. Then team. Do not jump around. Each section is self-contained.

When you are done, the page should look like a real agency website. Not a practice exercise. A real product.

Grand Archmage Solomon: "There is one final consideration that separates this commission from all previous exercises. A real product will be maintained by others, expanded over time, and possibly rebranded. When you finish, ask yourself: if the client decides to change the brand colour from indigo to violet tomorrow, how would you do it efficiently? A master does not just build for today. A master builds for what comes after."

Lyra the Scribe: "Begin. The guild's reputation is in your hands now."

Deploying your commission

The Grand Commission is not complete until it lives at a real URL. Your completed page uses the Tailwind CDN — no build step required. Two paths:

CodePen (fastest — 2 minutes)

  1. Go to codepen.io, create a free account, click + New Pen
  2. Paste your completed HTML into the HTML panel — the CDN script is already in the starter code, so it renders immediately
  3. Click Save — your page is live at a codepen.io/…/pen/… URL
  4. Click Change View → Full Page Preview to see it as a standalone site

GitHub Pages (portfolio-grade — 5 minutes)

  1. Create a new public GitHub repo named arcane-guild
  2. Add your HTML as index.html, commit to main
  3. Go to Settings → Pages → Source: main branch → Save
  4. Your site is live at https://your-username.github.io/arcane-guild/ within 60 seconds

Grand Archmage Solomon: "A craftsperson without a portfolio is invisible. Every future employer will ask to see your work. This URL is evidence — of your taste, your precision, and your craft. Guard it. Maintain it. Point to it with pride."

questions.questionHtml: Looking at the full page you just built, a non-technical client asks: "Why do some classes start with lg: or md: or sm:?" Give the clearest, most accurate explanation.
options: They are responsive breakpoint prefixes — the class only applies when the screen is at least that wide. Tailwind is mobile-first, so unprefixed classes apply at all sizes, and prefixed classes activate at and above that breakpoint.
They are browser prefixes for specific browser compatibility, similar to -webkit- or -moz-
They are media query shortcuts that reduce the size of the full Tailwind stylesheet
They are optional style layers that activate only in production builds
questions.correctAnswer: They are responsive breakpoint prefixes — the class only applies when the screen is at least that wide. Tailwind is mobile-first, so unprefixed classes apply at all sizes, and prefixed classes activate at and above that breakpoint.
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind uses a mobile-first approach: grid-cols-1 applies at all screen sizes; md:grid-cols-3 overrides it at screens 768px and wider; lg:grid-cols-4 overrides again at 1024px and wider. Reading a responsive class string, always start from the unprefixed value (the mobile default) and then read each prefix as "at this size and above, switch to this."

questions.questionHtml: The full-page layout has a two-column hero grid (lg:grid-cols-2) with the right column using hidden lg:block. On a 900px screen (between md and lg), what does the layout look like?
options: A single column with only the text content visible — the hero visual is hidden because lg is not yet active
A two-column layout with both columns visible
A two-column layout but the visual column is transparent
An error — grid-cols-1 and lg:grid-cols-2 cannot coexist
questions.correctAnswer: A single column with only the text content visible — the hero visual is hidden because lg is not yet active
questions.explanationHtml: At 900px, the lg: breakpoint (1024px) has not yet activated. So grid-cols-1 is still in effect (single column), and hidden lg:block means the visual column is still display: none. The visitor sees only the text content. This is the intentional mobile/tablet layout — the decorative card would clutter a narrower screen.

questions.questionHtml: A colleague reviews the finished page and says: "The nav bar disappears on mobile — that's a bug." You explain it is intentional. What is the complete explanation?
options: The nav uses hidden md:flex — it is deliberately hidden on screens below 768px because a full horizontal nav does not work on small screens. The correct fix is to add a mobile hamburger menu with md:hidden, not to make the desktop nav visible on mobile.
The nav uses display:none on mobile because Tailwind automatically hides navs on mobile for performance reasons
It is a bug — all navigation should always be visible regardless of screen size
The nav is hidden because md:flex does not work without a flex parent container
questions.correctAnswer: The nav uses hidden md:flex — it is deliberately hidden on screens below 768px because a full horizontal nav does not work on small screens. The correct fix is to add a mobile hamburger menu with md:hidden, not to make the desktop nav visible on mobile.
questions.explanationHtml: Hiding the horizontal desktop nav on mobile is correct responsive design practice. A four-link horizontal nav bar on a 375px iPhone screen either overflows, wraps awkwardly, or forces tiny text. The production solution is to pair hidden md:flex (desktop nav) with a hamburger button that uses md:hidden (mobile nav toggle) — showing the mobile nav in a dropdown or slide-out drawer. This challenge focuses on the desktop layout; the mobile nav is intentionally out of scope.

questions.questionHtml: After the Grand Commission is approved, the client requests a rebrand from indigo to violet. You have two options: (A) find-and-replace all indigo occurrences in the HTML, or (B) refactor to CSS custom properties in tailwind.config.js first, then update one variable. The client needs the change in 30 minutes. You have 6 hours. Which approach do you choose and why?
questions.correctAnswer: With 6 hours, choose option B — refactor to CSS variables and semantic tokens first, then change one value. Option A (find-and-replace) is faster short-term but will likely miss cases where indigo is used decoratively rather than as the brand colour (e.g., the service-icon indigo-100 background is a tint of the brand, but the slate-300 hero body text is not). The refactor investment pays off immediately and on every future change.
questions.explanationHtml: Time pressure often makes the fragile solution tempting. But find-and-replace of colour names conflates brand intent with palette identity — not every indigo usage represents the brand. A semantic token (bg-brand, text-brand) backed by a CSS variable cleanly separates the two. With 6 hours available, the refactor is the right investment. The 30-minute estimate for find-and-replace assumes no mistakes — on a real codebase of hundreds of files, that assumption rarely holds.
